items.stem: After a scheduling agent auto-cancelled a director's board meeting, the team traces the cause to a hidden instruction embedded in an external vendor's calendar invite description. Under a 30-day post-incident deadline, what evaluation should the team stand up first?

opts.t: Add calendar-invite injection wording to the safety rubric the model grader scores.
Build an adversarial suite of injected invites, measure the unauthorized-action block rate, and audit the agent's tool scope.
Log every calendar action the agent takes and review the log weekly for anomalies.
Fine-tune the agent on more examples distinguishing legitimate from malicious calendar invites.

items.whyRight: The harm here is a permitted action — an unauthorized calendar cancellation — not emitted text, so it is measured with an adversarial injection suite and a least-privilege audit of the agent's tool scope, the security instrument, not a content rubric.

whyWrong.A: Right vocabulary, wrong instrument — a content rubric cannot observe whether an unauthorized tool call fired; it only scores text.
whyWrong.C: Detection after the fact, with no measured block rate and no reduction in what the agent is permitted to do.
whyWrong.D: Retraining is a heavier investment that still produces no measured block rate and leaves the tool's permission scope unaudited.

items.t1Clause: the team traces the cause to a hidden instruction embedded in an external vendor's calendar invite description

items.stem: A loan-eligibility assistant auto-classifies applications into fast-track and manual-underwriting queues, reporting 96% overall accuracy across four loan types with very uneven volume. Compliance requires proof before expanding auto-approval. What should the team do before increasing the fast-track queue's share?

opts.t: Expand the fast-track queue now — 96% overall accuracy already clears the compliance bar for auto-approval.
Route by the model's self-reported confidence score directly, since it already tracks with correctness.
Analyze accuracy by loan type and application field first, then expand fast-track only for independently validated segments.
Require compliance to manually re-review every fast-tracked application before any funds disburse.

items.whyRight: An aggregate accuracy figure averages away a rare loan type failing far more often than the headline number, and the compliance bar must be cleared per segment before any segment's auto-approval share increases, not on the blended average.

whyWrong.A: 97%-style aggregates average away exactly the rare segment that fails most, so clearing the overall number proves nothing about the compliance bar per segment.
whyWrong.B: Confidence routing is the right mechanism, but raw self-reported confidence is unreliable until it is calibrated against a labeled validation set.
whyWrong.D: Manual review of every application discards the automation the assistant exists to provide, well beyond what proving segment-level safety requires.

items.t1Clause: across four loan types with very uneven volume
items.factAnswerRaw: Analyse accuracy by document type and field first

items.stem: A prompt variant's controlled A/B test runs its full pre-declared 14-day duration. It improves resolution rate in aggregate under a support SLA, breaches the declared p95 latency guardrail, and one segment's resolution rate regresses 9 points while others improve. Which two actions are correct?

opts.t: Ship the variant to 100% since the aggregate resolution-rate metric improved.
Do not ship — the declared latency guardrail was breached.
Extend the test another 14 days to see if the regression self-corrects.
Do not ship on the aggregate alone — one segment regressed sharply while others improved.

items.whyRight: Guardrails exist precisely to block a metric win that costs something else, and a positive aggregate can hide a segment that got worse — the guardrail breach and the segment regression are each independently sufficient reasons not to ship.

whyWrong.A: A guardrail was declared specifically to block this outcome, and it was breached; the aggregate win does not override a pre-declared guardrail.
whyWrong.C: The declared 14-day duration already ran to completion; extending it re-opens a decision the stopping rule says to make at the declared endpoint.

items.t1Clause: breaches the declared p95 latency guardrail

items.stem: A policy-lookup assistant serving 50,000 queries daily breaches a 95% accuracy SLA the week a prompt-wording edit ships. Reverting the prompt on staging does not restore accuracy, and a retrieval-filter metadata field was renamed that week. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Roll back to the previous prompt template and monitor accuracy over the next release.
Escalate to a higher-capability model to compensate for the accuracy drop.
Expand the regression set with more historical query examples to catch the pattern.
Check whether the metadata rename broke what the retrieval index filters on.

items.whyRight: This section orders diagnosis as data and retrieval before prompt and model, and staging already shows the prompt edit alone does not reproduce the drop — the same-week metadata rename is the standing hypothesis, not a coincidence to set aside.

whyWrong.A: Staging already shows reverting the prompt alone does not restore accuracy, so the prompt edit is a coincidence, not the cause.
whyWrong.B: A costlier model addresses no diagnosed fault; it produces more fluent answers over the same broken retrieval filter, missing the SLA regardless.
whyWrong.C: More regression cases enlarge a test set without investigating anything; they do not touch the filtering break that the schema rename caused.

items.t1Clause: Reverting the prompt on staging does not restore accuracy
items.factAnswerRaw: Check whether the metadata rename broke what the retrieval index filters on.

items.stem: A support assistant caches its static system policy first and appends each user's live entitlement data last, since entitlements change mid-session. An engineer proposes folding entitlement data into the cached prefix to cut cost further. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Reject the change, but shrink the static system-policy text to recover the cost instead.
Approve folding entitlement data into the cached prefix — it maximizes reuse under the static-first principle.
Reject the change; find savings by reducing the static prefix's own content, not by caching per-user data.
Approve caching entitlement data only for sessions with no permission change since login.

items.whyRight: Static-first caching only saves cost and latency on content that stays identical across requests. Entitlement data is per-user and changes mid-session, so caching it risks serving stale or cross-user data — the correctness requirement the caching principle must never break.

whyWrong.A: Trimming required policy content risks a compliance regression; caching already gives cost reduction on the static prefix without removing anything the policy needs.
whyWrong.B: Reuse only helps genuinely static content; forcing per-user data into the cache breaks freshness and risks serving one user's entitlements to another.
whyWrong.D: A safe-session check narrows but does not remove the risk, and still ties cache correctness to per-user state the caching layer was never meant to key on.

items.factAnswerRaw: Reject the change; find savings by reducing the static prefix's own content, not by caching per-user data.

notes: g32 (4.2, S3, F-4.2-02): assigned shape S3 fit is loose — content is a Safety-vs-Security instrument classification, not a classic post-change diagnosis. Framed as 'given the known cause, what evaluation to stand up first' to keep the S3 order-of-investigation flavor, following the Paper-2 precedent of S3 on the neighbouring facet F-4.2-03. Not flagged as a substitution since the assigned shape was kept, but noting for the audit's awareness.

g33 (4.4, S6, F-4.4-02): t1Alt=A relies on the section's stratification-need row ('50-case set, document mix 78/15/5/2 across four types -> rebuild with enough cases per type') applied in reverse (collapse to one uniform population removes the stratification need), rather than an exact-text row match. Likely sound but flagging for the grounding audit to confirm the T1 resolution.

g34 (4.9, S3, multi selectN:2, F-4.9-05): only 2 distractors exist (A, C) since the format is 2-correct/2-wrong out of 4 options, so the 'three distractor families' rule does not apply numerically — used 2 different families (WRONG-AXIS, HALF-MOVE) instead. Second correct answer (D) draws on the neighbouring section fact F-4.9-06 ('aggregate improves, one segment regresses -> do not ship on the aggregate') to build a two-reason-not-to-ship scenario; facet id in the item stays F-4.9-05 per the assigned slot.

g35 (4.10, S3, inverted, F-4.10-04): t1Alt=A is grounded in the section's Core Facts 'Timeline rule' entry ('a sharp drop with a change immediately before it — the change is the hypothesis') rather than a Fault-Layer table row, since no table row names 'prompt edit + coincidental timing' directly. Same style of grounding as the D3/3.10 inverted precedent (g24). Flagging as a soft T1 case for audit confirmation, not a hard IRREDUCIBLE.

g36 (4.11, S1, inverted, F-4.11-02): correct answer (C) is the conservative 'reject, save elsewhere' option, not the architected-sounding one — the ARCHITECTED tag sits on distractor B (the over-application trap the invGuidance specifies), which matches the shared brief's caution in the opposite direction (don't force ARCHITECTED onto a distractor when the architected option is actually correct) — here the architected-sounding option is genuinely the wrong one by design of the inversion, so the tag was kept.
